Finally, we construct a thermal graph aware of through-silicon vias (TSVs) that bounds the walk's jump rate while retaining the anisotropic conduction of TSV arrays. Experiments on periodic 2.5D/3D IC benchmarks show that, at equal accuracy, CycleWalker achieves up to 75.85X speedup over the transient random-walk solver.

title: Generalized Tensor Parallelism: Powering Trillion-Parameter LLM Training at 10+ EFLOP/s
summary: Pretraining state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) with up to trillions of parameters is memory- and compute-intensive. Existing parallelization schemes compromise on either per-GPU memory or throughput: data parallelism replicates parameters; tensor parallelism and fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) add communication of activations and parameters, respectively, to every microbatch; and pipeline parallelism leaves GPUs idle while the pipeline fills and drains. We show that, for linear layers, five commonly used parallelisms (data, tensor, sequence, context parallelism and FSDP) are special cases of one framework, generalized tensor parallelism (GTP), in which each layer's parameters and activations are partitioned and either can be re-materialized with an all-gather before use. In GTP, a parameter all-gather is an optional preprocessing step on one input of a matrix multiplication (GEMM), whereas FSDP implementations typically treat it as a step before an entire Transformer block, which can increase memory footprint and delay GEMMs. The GTP view lets us schedule all-gathers per GEMM rather than per block, issuing each early enough to hide its communication but late enough to limit memory. Our implementation is open source at https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM; with it, an internal 2T-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model reaches \textbf{13.0 model EFLOP/s} (exaFLOP/s) on 12,288 GB300 GPUs with 98\% weak-scaling efficiency, and runs with 1M-token sequences on 512 GPUs. On 256--1,024 GPUs, our implementation achieves \textbf{1.05--1.55$\times$ the throughput of Megatron-FSDP} across three MoE models and \textbf{1.27--1.31$\times$ that of a tuned 3D-parallel recipe with pipeline parallelism} on a DeepSeek-V4-Pro proxy model.

title: Machine-Learning-Assisted Hybrid Cooling of a Raspberry Pi 5
summary: Thermal management is a critical challenge in compact computing platforms operating under sustained high computational loads. Elevated processor temperatures can lead to thermal throttling, degraded performance, and reduced reliability. This study develops and experimentally evaluates a smart hybrid heat sink that integrates passive thermal energy storage with active cooling for sustained device operation. The proposed design comprises an aluminum cavity containing paraffin wax as a phase change material (PCM) embedded within a copper foam and integrated with an adaptively controlled fan. Fan operation is guided by a Random Forest regression model trained on experimentally measured CPU temperature data to predict future CPU temperatures. The predicted temperature is then used to support the adaptive fan control strategy. The heat sink is mounted directly on the CPU of a Raspberry Pi 5 and experimentally evaluated under an extreme CPU workload of approximately 99 percent CPU utilization. The performance of the proposed hybrid system is compared against two benchmark scenarios: passive cooling using PCM embedded in copper foam and a commercial Raspberry Pi 5 active cooler. The proposed heat sink demonstrates superior thermal performance to both benchmarks, achieving peak CPU temperature reductions of approximately 9 C relative to the PCM-copper foam configuration and 6 C relative to the commercial active cooler.

title: FlashQLA: Efficient Context Parallelism for Gated DeltaNet
summary: Gated DeltaNet (GDN) achieves linear computational complexity through recurrent state updates, but sequential dependencies between chunks limit parallelism, particularly for long-context workloads with small batch sizes or limited head-level parallelism per GPU. We present FlashQLA, a context-parallel execution framework for GDN that exposes additional sequence-level parallelism while reducing boundary-state preprocessing overhead. FlashQLA reduces boundary-state preprocessing overhead through decay-aware preparation and extends sequence parallelism across GPUs with Dual CP, which shares summary computation across parallelism levels. Workload-adaptive Auto CP and CP-aware kernel co-design further improve execution efficiency. FlashQLA achieves $1.7\times$-$3.1\times$ forward speedup and up to $4.4\times$ backward speedup over Flash Linear Attention (FLA) on a single GPU. On eight GPUs with context lengths up to 1M tokens, Dual CP achieves up to $4.8\times$ forward speedup and $4.4\times$ speedup for combined forward and backward execution over FLA KCP.

title: Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums: Execution-Bound Evidence Certification and Plausible-World Safety Gating in Agentic Control Planes
summary: Agreement among large language models is not physical evidence for mutating production infrastructure. Because generative models share pretraining priors and conform to peer rationales during deliberation, voting ensembles correlate errors instead of providing independent fault tolerance; yet attaching rigid deterministic checks to unconstrained agent outputs paralyzes incident remediation. We present Provenance-Isolated Epistemic Quorums (PIEQ), an execution-bound certification layer that keeps every language model strictly outside the trusted computing base. PIEQ unifies assumption-based truth maintenance, physical provenance isolation, control-theoretic plausible-world safety shielding, and linearizable concurrency governance around three distinct obligations: certifying diagnostic preconditions from disjoint physical failure domains, gating candidate mutations across all unrefuted fault worlds while falling back to read-only diagnostic probes under ambiguity, and binding admission certificates to target execution through snapshot barriers, revision checks, authorization freshness, trusted temporal-precondition policies, and capability-tiered enforcement. Across formal guarantees, automated etcd fault suites, frozen software benchmarks, and live language-model runs, PIEQ achieves zero within-assumption unsafe admissions and zero false-precondition commits, converting occasional agent proof omissions into recoverable false blocks rather than unsafe actions. On a physical PostgreSQL/Patroni cluster, PIEQ gates supervised failovers alongside Patroni and etcd's native split-brain protection and enforces a full Tier E2 contract inside a single serializable PostgreSQL transaction for bounded capacity reservations. All benchmarks are author-labeled, live model snapshots are unpinned, and Tier E2 physical failover promotion as well as multi-host hardware fault isolation remain open work.

title: APQKE-DR: Entropy-Failure Analysis of a Post-Quantum-Initialized Ratcheted Channel
summary: Long-lived secure channels for embedded and cyber-physical systems (CPSs) must resist quantum attacks and failures in endpoint randomness. While several post-quantum key exchange protocols exist, their security assumes reliable randomness at the endpoint, but this assumption is not always true in embedded devices. In this paper, we introduce the Entropy Attack Suite (EAS) to evaluate secure channels facing endpoint randomness failures, such as low-entropy boot and Random Number Generation (RNG) path subversion. As a case study, we design and implement APQKE-DR, a post-quantum secure channel. Its handshake uses ML-KEM [1] and ML-DSA [2], producing a root key for an X25519 Double Ratchet. We assess the performance of APQKE-DR and security for smart grid communication, and integrate it beneath ANSI C12.22 and DNP3 without altering payload formats. On a Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5, the APQKE handshake exchanges 9,610 bytes with median latencies of 1.99 ms (node) and 0.82 ms (server). The ratcheted channel adds 31 bytes per message. With fresh randomness and ideal cryptographic primitives, ProVerif verifies the modeled secrecy and authentication properties. If randomness fails, EAS can recover the RNG stream and root key from public transcripts. Under RNG-path subversion, a weak generator exposes the root key across sessions. If subversion also affects X25519 keys, attackers may access ratchet keys and plaintexts. TPM seeding prevents early-boot attacks but not later subversion, while measured boot can block modified firmware. Secure deployment thus requires integrity along the entire entropy path, not just strong cryptographic primitives.

title: When Online Adaptation of Resilience Policies Hurts: Safe Exploration and Measurement Pitfalls in Resilience4j
summary: Circuit breaker, retry, and bulkhead settings in Java microservices are tuned once and frozen, although the best setting depends on the fault a dependency is currently showing. We study whether an online learner can pick these settings at runtime. AdaptR4j swaps Resilience4j policies atomically in Spring Boot 3 and lets a contextual bandit choose among complete CircuitBreaker/Retry/Bulkhead configurations from Prometheus signals. Our first, naive design scored worse than keeping the default policy in three of four winnable fault scenarios under the reward it optimised: exploring a menu that contained aggressive circuit breakers rejected most traffic while the learner was still learning. Two safeguards fix this: a safe policy menu (no breaker stricter than the latency SLO) and safe exploration with a bounded reward. With them, AdaptR4j beats the production default in every winnable scenario (p < 0.001, three runs each, run-to-run SD <= 0.03), beats the best fixed policy when the fault changes over time, and cuts user-visible failures up to 3.7x compared with the naive design. A context-free bandit on the same safe menu performs statistically indistinguishably, so the safeguards - not the learner - carry most of the benefit. We also report how an earlier version of our harness produced convincing but wrong results: a unit mismatch made every circuit breaker 100x too strict and rejected calls were invisible to the metrics, so 94% of user requests failed while latency and error metrics looked excellent.

title: LIBRA: Runtime Co-Tuning of Batch Size and Parallelism for Time-Efficient LLM Training
summary: Training large language models (LLMs) requires choosing both a batch size and a parallel configuration. Existing systems make these decisions in isolation, tuning parallelism for throughput and batch size for convergence, but neither objective alone determines training efficiency. We present LIBRA, a lightweight runtime framework that co-tunes batch size and parallel configuration to minimize end-to-end time. LIBRA treats throughput and convergence as two noisy objectives and searches their joint space using parallel noisy expected hypervolume improvement (qNEHVI). To make this runtime search efficient, we propose hierarchical pruning, which removes infeasible and low-throughput parallel configurations through system-level performance estimation and then narrows batch-size candidates through critical-batch-size-aware convergence monitoring. We further design acquisition-guided parallel evaluation (AGPE), which evaluates surviving candidates concurrently across GPU groups in order of their acquisition values. On clusters of up to 256 GPUs, LIBRA reduces time-to-convergence by 31.1% on average over state-of-the-art methods, while runtime tuning accounts for only 0.3-3.5% of overall time.

title: Network-Guided Automated Synthesis of MAC Units for Neural Network Inference
summary: In neural inference accelerators, multiply-accumulate (MAC) datapaths account for the majority of circuit area and critical-path delay, where operator-level numerical formats simultaneously dictate hardware overhead and quantization error. Yet no straightforward mapping exists between hardware cost and end-to-end network accuracy: logic synthesis transforms datapaths in a highly nonlinear manner, while numerical errors propagate and couple across layers. To address this disconnect, we present NAMSI, an automated network-aware MAC synthesis framework tailored for neural inference. NAMSI characterizes heterogeneous data formats using a format-distribution representation (FD) and leverages topology-aware accuracy and hardware-cost modeling (TaH), calibrated with actual post-synthesis Area-Delay Product (ADP) measurements, to jointly estimate coupled full-network accuracy and circuit cost. Furthermore, reversible lattice search (RLS) is introduced to tractably navigate the exponentially scaling design space. Evaluations across five neural networks on ImageNet-1K demonstrate that under post-training quantization (PTQ), NAMSI achieves 54.2%-60.4% reductions in post-synthesis MAC ADP compared with FP32 while retaining at least 99% of full-precision Top-1 accuracy, surpassing baseline approaches in both hardware efficiency and accuracy preservation.

title: Discovering Bandwidth-Efficient Prefetchers to Shrink the Cache Hierarchy
summary: Shared last-level caches (LLCs) increasingly dominate server processor die area, forcing architects to trade core counts for cache capacity. While intelligent data prefetching offers a pathway to reclaim this silicon, designing coordinated, multi-level prefetching policies for multi-core systems is bottlenecked by day-long, cycle-level simulations. This simulation wall limits even LLM-based microarchitecture discovery; the state-of-the-art ArchAgent system evolves one cache level at a time on single-core benchmarks, adds multi-core configurations only at the end, and trails the human champion under multi-core shared cache contention. We introduce DuoArchitect, an autonomous agentic framework for multi-fidelity, multi-core co-discovery of prefetchers. Agents jointly evolve evaluation proxies and coordinated prefetching policies across the L1D, L2, and LLC hierarchies, constructing simulation proxies 3-26x faster than cluster evaluation and hardware diagnostic oracles to guide the search. To study how much cache silicon a smarter prefetcher can replace, we evaluate and evolve prefetchers under reduced cache budgets, and find that evolving under our tightest cache constraint (with both the L2 and LLC halved) produced our strongest prefetcher overall at every cache size we tested: DuoArch-Nano. On the Fourth Data Prefetching Championship (DPC4) benchmarks with full-size caches, DuoArch-Nano delivers a 9.2% geomean IPC speedup (+10.5% on four-core mixes) while reducing four-core DRAM traffic by 11.4%, more than doubling the gains of the human champion BertiGO and the agentic ArchAgent v2. When the LLC is halved, DuoArch-Nano erases the baseline's 8.6% overall slowdown and edges out the full-LLC baseline overall (+0.88%), showing that agentic frameworks can generate prefetchers that reclaim megabytes of LLC SRAM per core with zero overall IPC penalty.

title: Native Block-Quantized Matrix Multiplication and Explicit K/V Residency with Dual-View Access for LLM Inference on RISC-V Vector Processors
summary: Some key execution states in large language model inference persist across multiple instructions and are difficult to express and exploit within RVV semantics centered on individual operations. We define specialization boundaries according to data-state lifetimes and propose Quantized Block Streams (QBS) and Attention/KV Context (AKV) while preserving RVV programmability. QBS organizes native-block format processing, block traversal, integer computation, and ordered FP32 accumulation into a unified execution process, whereas AKV maintains local K/V residency and supplies operand views aligned with the computation direction while leaving Attention arithmetic on RVV. Cycle-accurate RTL evaluation shows that QBS achieves geometric-mean speedups of 35.68x and 51.34x for projection Compute and Matmul, respectively, while AKV achieves a 1.45x geometric-mean speedup over Tiled RVV for Decode Attention. Compared with the baseline, the complete design increases total area by 12.65%; on the evaluated projection workloads, throughput per area and energy efficiency improve by 46.63x and 19.78x, respectively. Further evaluation demonstrates applicability across multiple block-quantization formats and across models with different Attention organizations.

title: Multi Agent Reinforcement Learning enhanced Federated Learning for Predicting Remaining Useful Lifetime
summary: Remaining useful life (RUL) prediction is central to Prognostics and Health Management (PHM). The growth of industrial IoT has unlocked large multivariate sensor streams and enabled deep models - especially Transformers - for long-horizon sequence learning. However, transformers are parameter-heavy and data-hungry, while operational datasets are often siloed and privacy-sensitive. Federated Learning (FL) addresses this by training across clients without raw data sharing, but in practice many clients connect over lossy wireless links where UDP is preferred for low latency, making model exchange vulnerable to packet drops. We present a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) framework that adapts FL to lossy channels by selecting per-client layer subsets to transmit and capping retransmissions. This framework is trained with QMIX value-function factorization for scalability. We instantiate the approach with a Graph Convolution Position-Aware Transformer (GCPATr) for RUL forecasting. On the CMAPSS dataset, our MARL-enhanced FL (RL-FL) consistently improves mean square error over standard FL, with the largest gains at high packet loss (e.g., up to 18% improvement on FD003 at 50% loss). These results show that MARL is an effective countermeasure to wireless degradation in FL-based RUL prediction.

title: AgentDRC: Multi-Agent Algorithms for Spatially-Aware Automated DRC Correction
summary: Design Rule Checking (DRC) error fixing remains a time-consuming bottleneck in physical design, often requiring manual intervention despite advanced EDA optimizations. Existing LLM-agent approaches fall short due to redundant contextual shapes, limited spatial reasoning over raw coordinates, and inefficient flat layout representations. We propose AgentDRC, which formulates iterative DRC correction as a multi-agent algorithm and introduces a spatial-aware verification and correction algorithm that reconstructs structured spatial relations among critical shapes and validates fixes through geometric and semantic constraint checking. The system coordinates four specialized agents to perceive multi-level, multi-modal geometric features, filter irrelevant shapes, and iteratively correct violations. Experiments show that AgentDRC achieves up to 30.4% pass@1 and 55.7% pass@5 on challenging violations, with 13.8% pass@5 improvement over the best baseline. We will open-source all code and benchmark tasks upon acceptance.

title: RankServe: Rank-Aware CPU-GPU Scheduling for Memory-Constrained MoE Serving
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity through sparse expert activation, but their large expert pools impose substantial memory requirements during inference. Low-rank compression reduces the memory footprint of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. However, the heterogeneous expert ranks create unequal storage, transfer, and execution costs. Under limited GPU memory, expert popularity and transfer cost alone cannot determine which experts are most valuable to retain. We present RankServe, a CPU-GPU serving system for compressed MoE checkpoints with fixed expert ranks. Its key insight is to value GPU residency against the cheaper nonresident path, CPU execution or weight transfer followed by GPU execution, under each expert's rank and token load. RankServe aggregates the resulting estimated savings over routing demand and prioritizes experts by savings per byte. It updates residency from recent routing history and selects miss paths using current token loads, allowing temporary GPU execution without cache admission. A variable-rank runtime executes heterogeneous factors through grouped matrix multiplications without common-rank padding. Implemented on vLLM, RankServe is evaluated on three MoE models against six serving systems on a single CPU-GPU platform. Across five batch sizes from 1 to 32, it achieves per-model geometric-mean speedups of $1.69$--$2.29\times$ in time to first token (TTFT) and $1.71$--$2.48\times$ in time per output token (TPOT), relative to the fastest baseline for each configuration and metric.

title: Accelerating Equivariant Interatomic Potentials for Molecular Dynamics through Radial tabulation and Kernel Fusion
summary: Equivariant machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) achieve near-quantum-chemical accuracy, but their computational cost and GPU memory footprint restrict molecular dynamics (MD) at extended length and time scales. Even when the tensor product (TP) is accelerated, both bottlenecks remain governed by evaluating and storing per-edge radial weights in the NequIP convolution. We introduce JET-MLIPs (Joint-Kernel Equivariant Convolution with Tabulated Radial Weights for MLIP simulation), a GPU backend applicable to pretrained NequIP-family potentials without retraining. JET-MLIPs replaces the radial multilayer perceptron (MLP) with a piecewise cubic Hermite table and fuses table lookup, spherical harmonics, TP and neighbor aggregation into a single kernel, eliminating per-edge radial-weight and MLP-intermediate storage during force evaluation. Across 15 released potentials from SevenNet, MACE, NequIP-OAM, Nequix and EquFlash on a 5632-atom liquid electrolyte, LAMMPS MD attains 1.5-5.9$\times$ step-time speed-ups and 2.4-24$\times$ peak memory reductions relative to each family's existing TP-accelerated backend on a single H200 GPU while preserving single-precision (fp32) accuracy and dynamical stability. These reductions enable multi-nanosecond transport-property simulations of roughly $10^4$-atom systems on a single GPU and broaden access to large-scale equivariant MLIP MD on widely available GPUs.

title: DELTA: Diagnosing Exploration Lineages via Twin-path Alignment - What Can Contrasting Design Paths Reveal About Microarchitectural Behavior?
summary: Architects have two mature instruments for performance work. Top-Down analysis tells them where a design loses its pipeline slots, and design-space exploration (DSE) tells them which configuration scores best. Neither explains why a search stops improving: why a backend-bound design rejects a prefetcher that the bottleneck label recommends, or why a capacity increase that helped in one configuration hurts in the next. This paper argues that the evidence needed to answer such questions is already produced during exploration and then discarded. Every parent-child edge in an exploration tree is a controlled intervention: one knob changes, the rest of the design is held fixed, and a cycle-level simulator measures the outcome. When the same edit helps under one parent and hurts under another, aligning the two parents localizes the interaction that decides its sign. We present DELTA, a simulator-grounded root-cause analysis tool that builds a Design Memory of such interventions during exploration and lets an architect query it afterwards. Each record stores the full parent configuration, the single applied edit, the measured and predicted IPC, a Top-Down breakdown from StallLens, our gem5 implementation of Top-Down, and its lineage. Unlike evolutionary LLM search, which keeps only high-scoring programs, DELTA keeps failed edges as evidence. The same memory also makes exploration efficient: on four SPEC CPU2017 workloads, the full system raises IPC by 55.5% in 22 simulated designs for $1.56 of model cost, predicts the IPC of its own proposals to within 3.3%, and keeps improving after a bottleneck-guided search stalls. A root-cause query over the recorded history led us to a usefulness-throttled variant of the Best-Offset prefetcher that improves IPC by 1.37% over the original in matched configurations.

title: Separating Measurement Failures from Defence Failures in Split Language-Model Privacy
summary: Split-training privacy evaluations fail through distinct mechanisms. Evaluators can overlook an exposed gradient channel, align reconstructions against shifted labels, or deploy uncalibrated probes before testing a candidate defence, while calibrated attacks can also refute real defences. Separating these failure modes alters which claims survive. We conduct a retrospective evidentiary reanalysis across four split-LLM campaigns and two cross-cutting scope checks covering host key custody and variational mutual-information bounds, mapping every recorded claim to one of five admissibility states (breach, non-detection, undetermined coverage, invalid measurement, or out-of-scope inference). Across a 19-configuration exploration, only four of 24 required probes qualified, yet those four calibrated probes still established qualified privacy breaches in 13 configurations, while utility or learning-gain failures eliminated the remaining 6. In a seven-cell defence-redesign pilot, 2 quantised configurations failed utility gates, calibrated next-byte structure probes breached the 0.02 gate on all 7 cells (0.097 to 0.112), and qualified punctuation-property probes reached 0.79 to 0.89, yielding 4 failed and 3 undetermined composite privacy assessments (the latter from marginal null-band excursions on punctuation bindings). Negative evidence against both defence families remains intact. Scope checks further show that shared-key orthogonal wrappers protect passive network captures without hiding activations from a compromised restoring host, and why near-zero variational lower bounds leave worst-case leakage unconstrained. Rerunnable scripts verify 1,522 checks across 122 SHA-256-pinned artifacts while preserving each campaign's native seed intervals and retrospective boundaries.

title: MOSAIC: Memory-Organized Search with Anti-Imitation Crossover for Training-Free Microarchitecture Optimization
summary: Large language models can generate cache-replacement policies. The central challenge is to retain performance on workloads excluded from the search. In our adaptations of published search methods, generated code resembles established policies, with cosine similarities of 0.78-0.84. The wider comparison also shows held-out harmonic-mean instructions-per-cycle (IPC) losses of 1.0-2.4%. We present MOSAIC, a search controller that improves policies without updating language-model weights. It stores concise lessons from previous evaluations rather than repeatedly copying high-scoring code. When improvement stops, it selects two high-scoring policies whose code embeddings differ and asks the model to combine their mechanisms. Novelty prompts and model rotation support this search; controlled memory edits test how the stored lessons affect later proposals. We evaluate cache replacement using intervention-level cross-validation and a wider comparison on ten memory-intensive SPEC2006 workloads. MOSAIC reaches a 51.1% peak hit rate on the primary search workload and a 47.9% held-out mean in the intervention study. Removing crossover reduces these values by 7.8 and 21.8 percentage points, respectively, whereas the tested stronger model improves the held-out mean by 0.4 points. In the wider IPC comparison, MOSAIC has the smallest held-out gap (0.31%) and the highest held-out IPC among the evaluated LLM configurations. Adapting the same controller to data prefetching gives a 4.8% mean speedup over the LRU reference configuration. The accompanying corpus contains 10,687 generated policies with lineage and per-iteration prompt logs.

title: fork() for Agents: Agent Kernel for Non-blocking LLM Orchestration
summary: LLM-based agents typically execute tool calls synchronously and discard completed work upon failure. Subgraph-selective recovery, re-executing only a failed node's transitive descendants, is a well-established pattern in distributed systems (Spark, Erlang/OTP, Dryad), and recent agent runtimes (Sherlock, AgentGit, Atomix) preserve completed work through verifiers, version control, or transactional tool boundaries. We present \textbf{Agent-Kernel}, a non-blocking runtime that ports this pattern to the LLM \emph{content plane}: its primitive, \textbf{Sub-Graph Recovery (SGR)}, fires on a raw exception with no trained verifier or planner, resets a failed node's descendants while preserving completed siblings, and composes each parent's text into its children's prompts (context inheritance), all on a durable substrate with a formal state-preservation guarantee. Across 14{,}434 runs on synthetic and standard benchmarks (tau-bench, Gaia2, AutomationBench, InterruptBench), SGR reaches full recovery within budget=3 where whole-trajectory replay exhausts (100\% vs.\ 55\%), and is roughly 10$\times$ faster than an adapted Sherlock rollback that also recovers. It matches ReAct-serial accuracy within noise on linear workloads while adding recovery and parallelism (up to 12.7$\times$ speedup) where structure permits. Ablation isolates SGR: removing it collapses success to 39.4\%.

title: RTLDetective: Agentic RTL Debugging through Dataflow Analysis and Simulation-Guided Fault Localization
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have shown promise in RTL debugging, yet accurately localizing functional errors and generating reliable repairs remain challenging. We propose RTLDetective, a multi-agent framework that integrates signal dependency analysis, simulation-guided fault localization, and knowledge-based reasoning for automated RTL debugging and repair. RTLDetective constructs signal dependency graphs from RTL code and extracts failure information from waveform traces. A lightweight localizer agent predicts expected intermediate signal values and evaluates them through targeted simulation interventions, iteratively probing signal dependencies to isolate suspicious logic and identify potential fault locations. A debug agent combines this evidence with static analysis, a curated knowledge base of hardware design principles and RTL bug patterns, and reasoning to generate corrected RTL. To reduce inference overhead, the framework reuses cached context across debugging iterations. We evaluate RTLDetective on the MEIC benchmark, achieving an 86.1% fix rate, 13.9 percentage points above the best baseline, while making fewer LLM calls.

title: Translation Validation of SystemVerilog-to-SystemC RTL Conversion by Reading the Generated C++
summary: SystemC models of register-transfer level (RTL) designs are used for virtual platforms, firmware bring-up and simulation without a commercial license, and more of them now come from translators and language models. A wrong model usually compiles, and it usually agrees with the RTL. SystemVerilog evaluates an 8-bit sum in 8 bits while C++ evaluates it in 64, so a translation that forgets one truncation keeps a carry the RTL drops, and only inputs near the top of the range show it. I built svcc, an open-source SystemVerilog-to-SystemC converter, and my first check of its output read the generated C++ with SystemVerilog's rules. That check passed two wrong models. The check that replaced it gives the generated header the meaning C++17 and SystemC give it and turns undefined behavior into proof obligations. It prints what it read as SystemVerilog with every width change explicit, then proves that equivalent to a netlist of the source by induction over registers matched by name. On 50 author-written designs it proves 45 and reports 5 as outside its model. In a mutation experiment it accepted none of the 17 mutants that compiled SystemC showed to be wrong. Of 2,184 modules from 16 open-source code bases, 1,185 conversions match Verilator in random co-simulation and the check proves 600 of them. The same runs found defects in the front end, in svcc and in Verilator.

title: AeroPoint: Agentic AI for Intent-Driven Point Cloud Inspection in UAV-Edge Systems
summary: Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV)-based Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) inspection generates dense point clouds that strain onboard computing and wireless bandwidth. Intent-based inspection allows operators to request objects, attributes, and spatial relationships through natural language. Answering these requests requires trans- lating intent into spatial queries and retrieving relevant evidence under UAV processing and communication constraints. This article presents AeroPoint, an agentic AI system combining onboard point cloud processing and knowledge graph construction with Large Language Model (LLM)-based retrieval planning at a ground edge server. The LLM translates inspection questions into structured requests, which the UAV executes to return selected graph evidence for answer generation. We evaluate the prototype in a power line inspection case study using 150 TS40K UAV LiDAR scenes and profile processing costs on NVIDIA Jetson Nano hardware. Retrieval experiments use graphs constructed from dataset-provided ground-truth semantic labels. Experimental results show that transmitted payload decreases from 3700 KB for complete point clouds to 3.1 KB for retrieval responses, while evaluated LLM routers achieve the highest graph retrieval completeness for relational queries.

title: When Coupling Backfires: BBR-Induced L4S Degradation under DualPI2
summary: Low Latency, Low Loss, Scalable Throughput (L4S) uses DualPI2 to separate low latency (e.g., TCP Prague) and Classic flows into two queues while coupling their congestion signals. However, this coupling is designed for Reno-like Classic congestion controls, while widely deployed BBR behaves differently. Prior studies observed severe Prague throughput degradation when BBR occupies the Classic queue under DualPI2, but the mechanism remains insufficiently explained. Through controlled testbed experiments and an extension of an existing BBRv1/BBRv2 fluid model with PI2, we show that BBR can drive the PI2 base probability p' far above CUBIC levels, producing strong coupled marking that can nearly starve Prague despite low L4S queueing delay. The model explains BBRv1's persistent high-p' regime, BBRv2's lower, oscillating p', and their dependence on the PI2 target relative to RTT. Additional experiments show that Prague throughput degradation also occurs with BBRv3. Our findings highlight the need for coupling mechanisms supporting low latency flows across heterogeneous Classic congestion controls.

title: Real-Time AI Acceleration on a 2D Spatial Dataflow Architecture
summary: Machine Learning (ML) is increasingly being integrated into real-time systems, which makes the timing analysis of ML accelerators necessary. However, the most popular commercial accelerator, the Graphics Processing Unit (GPU), remains difficult to analyze as several aspects of its behavior, including scheduling of threads involved in single-instruction multiple-thread computations and memory access latency, are not fully documented. Spatial dataflow accelerators present an interesting alternative to GPUs, as they inherently support compute and memory partitioning. Data movement and computation locality are explicitly controlled by the programmer. In this work, we consider the Tenstorrent Blackhole, which is based on a commodity RISC-V architecture. It consists of a 2D grid of cores connected by Networks-on-Chip (NoCs), supporting a fully open software runtime. We profile the Blackhole platform and develop a worst-case execution time task model as a Homogeneous Synchronous Dataflow Graph. We extend this model to a preliminary analysis of multi-core workloads by considering NoC-related delays. Finally, we evaluate our model across 12,567 task configurations and workloads. Results show that the estimate derived from our model lies above the observed worst case in every configuration. For single-core workloads, the overhead is less than 100% in most cases, with a maximum of less than 200%, and for multi-core workloads, it is less than 500% using a pessimistic NoC contention analysis. This paper lays the foundations for real-time computing on a promising open accelerator design.

title: Aftershock: Yesterday's Linux Kernel Bugs, Tomorrow's Android Exploits
summary: Android kernels have long suffered from slow patch propagation from Linux upstream, with fixes often reaching devices far later than conventional Linux distributions. Until recently, this lag was largely a patch-management problem. With rapidly improving LLM agents, it is becoming an exploitation problem: public upstream patches can now serve as blueprints for building working n-day exploits before downstream devices are fixed. We test this threat end to end by building an automated pipeline that screens upstream Linux patches, reproduces memory-safety vulnerabilities on Android targets, and drives an LLM agent to construct local privilege escalation exploits from an untrusted application. Across 152 candidate CVEs reported over 33 months, we reproduce 38 vulnerabilities and generate 17 independently verified exploits under production defenses. Exploitation takes a median of 14.3 agent-hours and $321 in API cost, with 90% median reliability; 12 of 14 trials succeed on Pixel 9 and Pixel 10 devices. Notably, the pipeline relies only on publicly available, off-the-shelf models. Surprisingly, only 3 of the 17 exploited CVEs appear in Android Security Bulletins, suggesting limited visibility into which upstream fixes address vulnerabilities that affect Android kernels. For these 17 CVEs, the corresponding upstream patches reach Pixel devices with a median delay of 181 days. Together, these results reveal a stark asymmetry: attackers can increasingly automate exploitation in hours, while defenders still identify and deploy fixes on the timescale of months.

title: ExitLUT: Boolean Early Exits for Efficient FPGA-Based Neural Network Inference
summary: Early exit neural networks reduce average inference cost by terminating once sufficient confidence is reached. On FPGAs, conventional confidence-based exits add arithmetic control paths poorly matched to LUT fabrics, consuming resources that could otherwise support the main datapath. We present ExitLUT, which replaces softmax-style exit decisions with learned Boolean functions mapped directly into FPGA LUTs. In our CNN evaluation, fpgaConvNet is the static spatial-dataflow baseline, while ATHEENA is its softmax-based early exit extension. ExitLUT reduces ATHEENA's exit-decision LUT usage by 2.58$\times$ over the softmax path and eliminates decision-path DSP usage, while preserving accuracy and exit behavior. Rerunning design-space exploration reinvests these savings into the datapath, improving throughput by up to 4.08$\times$ over fpgaConvNet and 1.82$\times$ over ATHEENA. For LUT-based NNs, embedded ExitLUT exits achieve 1.41-1.89$\times$ average time-to-decision speedup over static NeuraLUT-Assemble designs with under 1% LUT overhead.

title: TokenJoule: Energy Modeling for Distributed Training and Inference of LLMs
summary: As large language models (LLMs) scale, energy dictates operating cost, cooling, and cluster capacity across training and inference. Early hardware design-space exploration (DSE) requires predicting energy before silicon exists, yet performance models miss hidden component work while prior energy predictors calibrate to deployed GPUs. We present TokenJoule, an open-source analytical tool that derives device kernel sequences, tiled compute, shared-memory staging, cache residency, and collective traffic, pricing activity directly with component energies. With zero workload fitting, TokenJoule achieves 3.3-6.6% activity error (151 A100/H100 runs) and 3.0-6.8% A100 energy error, guiding parallelism, memory packaging, and 3D-DRAM chip co-design.

title: Pearl: TEE-Enabled Fair Ordering with Minimal Replication
summary: Recent research has investigated fair transaction ordering in blockchain consensus. An orthogonal line of work has demonstrated that equipping replicas with trusted execution environments (TEEs) enables more efficient consensus protocols with only $2f{+}1$ replicas. In this work, we bridge these two areas and demonstrate that two key fair-ordering properties, ordering linearizability and $γ$-batch-order fairness with minimal batching, cannot be implemented in partially synchronous networks with $2f{+}1$ replicas, even when the replicas are equipped with TEEs. We show that Byzantine replicas can circumvent TEE protections by manipulating the timing of transaction submissions to the enclave, thereby biasing the resulting ordering indicators. However, we prove that assuming a synchronous network allows both properties to be implemented with a reduced replica count. We propose two mechanisms: one uses absolute TEE-attested timestamps to guarantee ordering linearizability in a system of $n \ge 2f{+}1$ replicas, and the other uses TEE-maintained relative sequence numbers to guarantee $γ$-batch-order fairness when $n > \frac{2γf}{2γ-1}$. Ultimately, we integrate these mechanisms into a synchronous lane-based consensus algorithm, achieving strong fair-ordering properties and superior performance while requiring fewer replicas than representative state-of-the-art baselines.

title: Below the Stopwatch: Checking the Performance Claims of Coding Agents in the Kernel
summary: Coding agents open many pull requests (PRs) that claim to make software faster. Most such claims also give a reason, such as "cache the result" or "read the file once". A stopwatch can show that code got faster, but not that it got faster for the stated reason. We present Below, a pipeline that checks these reasons at the kernel level. From 1,343 runtime-performance PRs in the AIDev dataset, Below extracts the mechanism each PR claims and maps it to the kernel and hardware signals that must change if the claim is true. A build agent that never sees the claim rebuilds the code before and after each PR. Below then measures both versions with plain timing runs, hardware counters and LTTng kernel traces. Most claims are not measured: 57.3% of the PRs offer only reasoning or no evidence, and only 31.4% state an effect size. Of 82 analyzed PRs, 32 ran faster, 28 showed no clear change and 22 ran slower. The expected signal of the claimed mechanism appeared in 34 PRs (20 in kernel-trace signals alone), and 42 PRs also changed their output. Kernel signals move about 1.7 times as often for a faster PR's claimed mechanism as for mechanisms it did not claim; the instruction count barely separates them (1.15 times).

title: The Recycler: In-Transit Machine Learning on High-Fidelity Data from Simulation Campaigns as an Optimized Approach for Building Frontier Models
summary: We report on the first realization of in-transit machine learning using data streamed from multiple simulations running in parallel to the training on the same exascale high performance computing system. This workflow can be commonly applied to a broad variety of scenarios in which simulation campaigns play an important role. Unlike single simulations, campaigns run several simulations in parallel. This is interesting for finding an optimum operation point of a machine like a particle accelerator or a fusion reactor, quantifying the variation in model predictions e.g. in climate research, or discovering new capabilities e.g. in materials or drug design. Such campaigns produce huge amounts of high-fidelity data at high rates. File system bandwidth and capacity prohibit retaining all of that data, usually requiring orders of magnitude in reduction before it can be stored. We demonstrate a workflow that streams the data from multiple simulations to train a frontier model in parallel, thereby maximizing data throughput. We demonstrate that this can use a much larger amount of high-fidelity data as training data for the model compared to storage in files, essentially replacing file IO by in-transit training of large-scale frontier models. This will allow to create AI-informed feedback loops to steer simulation campaigns while reducing the overall computation time needed and provide high-fidelity frontier models for reuse by the scientific community.

title: Decoupling Faults from Uncertainty: Message-Efficient Byzantine Agreement with Local Predictions
summary: Byzantine Agreement protocols are traditionally designed under worst-case uncertainty about which processes are faulty, coupling the adversary's corruption budget $t$ with the system's epistemic uncertainty. Recent work showed that auxiliary failure predictions can improve round complexity, but cannot improve communication complexity when prediction errors are unconstrained. In this paper, we initiate a theoretical study of the complementary question: how much can Byzantine Agreement benefit when each process is guaranteed a local bound on its prediction error? We study this question through the local $k$-error prediction model, in which each process receives a local classification vector differing from the ground truth in at most $k$ positions. The predictions need not be common, and honest processes may hold substantially different views about whom to trust. Under this promise model -- where correctness relies on the local error bound holding -- we present a synchronous Byzantine Agreement algorithm requiring $n \ge t + 4k + 1$, where $n$ is the total number of processes, $t$ is the maximum number of failures, and $k$ is the local error bound per honest process. In the regime where local uncertainty is small ($k \ll t$), our protocol decouples communication from the total fault budget $t$: in an execution where the actual maximum prediction error is $s \le k$ and the actual number of failures is $f \le t$, the protocol terminates in $O(s+1)$ rounds and sends $O((f+k)ks + nk)$ honest messages, achieving $o(n^2)$ communication when $t = Θ(n)$ and $k = o(\sqrt{n})$. Finally, we show that it is not possible to solve Byzantine Agreement in the local $k$-error prediction model with fewer than $Ω(nk)$ honest messages.

title: Schism: Reconfigurable Scale-Up Domains for Distributed Quantum Computing
summary: Switch-based quantum datacenters connect quantum processing units (QPUs) through photonic switches and shared Bell-state measurement (BSM) devices. Sharing BSMs saves hardware, but fixed connectivity constrains access to these resources. Local communication can overload one rack's BSMs while others remain idle; reaching those idle resources incurs additional optical loss and retries through switches and quantum frequency converters (QFCs). Programs remain locked into this locality-contention tradeoff as their communication patterns change. We propose Schism, an architecture that lets programs dynamically change which QPUs share each BSM pool. Schism places BSM pools at aggregation switches and QFCs on their core-facing uplinks. Top-of-rack switches establish reconfigurable native-wavelength circuits from QPUs to these pools, forming scale-up domains bounded by the optical loss budget. Reconfiguration reshapes resource sharing across racks without moving QPUs or migrating quantum states. Our key insight is that QPU grouping jointly determines photon-path loss and contention for BSM resources: locality alone cannot identify the best grouping, and a grouping pays off only if its savings outweigh the delay of reconfiguring to it. We develop an optimization framework that combines graph partitioning with resource-constrained completion-time estimates and dynamic programming to select how QPUs share BSM pools and when those groupings reconfigure, between or within circuit phases. Our evaluation using SeQUeNCe with trapped-ion parameters shows that Schism achieves communication speedups of 4.9-7.3x across 11 workloads on 32 QPUs compared to Fixed Clos connectivity and 3.6-8.3x compared to SwitchQNet. Schism also outperforms a hypothetical network-wide switch by 1.35-1.38x on the eight workloads whose phases fit in a pool, and trails it by 1.1-1.75x on the other three.

title: Geometry, Reliability, and Spacetime Dynamics of Hyper-Simplex Fractal Networks
summary: Large-scale, delay-tolerant peer-to-peer networks that need strong consistency usually separate naming, routing, consensus, and ordering into independent layers. To bring deterministic network properties into complex peer-to-peer structures, we unify all four on a single recursive topology. Modeling mutual equality among N peers in Euclidean space requires dimension at least N-1, which prevents flat equal groups from scaling at fixed dimension. The hyper-simplex fractal network G(N,m) escapes this limit by recursion. Each non-leaf node anchors a half-scale N-clique. From the resulting digit-word addresses alone, nodes decide adjacency without routing tables, forward greedily along exact shortest paths, and converge geometrically to a self-similar attractor of dimension log_2 N. Running hierarchical PBFT on the same prefix tree achieves linear message load and logarithmic fault-free latency, with an explicit reliability threshold under independent faults and analytical recursions for anchor exposure, dual homing, and event registration. Reversible topology edits generate the Higman-Thompson group V_N on the address boundary, block order characterizes service-topology hosting beyond treewidth, and root-anchored block heights yield persistent spacetime coordinates with compact light-client proofs.

title: TideSand: Performance-Accurate Sandbox Multiplexing for LLM Agents
summary: We propose TideSand, a sandbox system that intelligently multiplexes resources for performance-sensitive LLM agents, such as auto research agents working on system measurement tasks. TideSand combines three key ideas: agent-aware scheduling, which schedules sandbox execution intelligently at the tool call level to avoid resource contention; speculative swapping, which offloads the memory of sandboxes waiting on inference and restores it before their next tool call; and selective rollback, which checkpoints selected sandboxes when contention occurs and restores them when machines are idle. We evaluate TideSand across six model-workload pairs on AlgoTune, Terminal-Bench 4.0, and Terminal-Bench Science. TideSand achieves 3.8-10x higher throughput than strict reservation while maintaining tool-call fidelity, or 7-44% higher fidelity than overcommit baselines at similar throughput. Moreover, TideSand reduces the evaluation error on Algotune by 19x through improved tool-call fidelity. We hope the work motivates future research to maintain tool call fidelity while keeping resource utilization high through statistical multiplexing.

title: A Systematic Method of GPU Verification on Subsystem Modelling
summary: ARM Fast Model is a software modelling system for simulating multiple systems IPs integrated in a subsystem. Fast Model allows customer to run whole software stack as early as system IPs' specification is just ready. In this paper, we talk about a systematic method to enable GPU modelling and make whole system software stacks executable for both CPU and GPU in the integrated modelling environment, and eventually the major GPU IP can be verified. With our solution, we can directly run commercial benchmarks like Antutu and GFX Bench in Android target system with underlying ARM Fast Model mobile subsystem support. This was unbelievable in the past due to 3D rendering simulation for GPU verification is very slow. We also introduce some special techniques to improve performance. Eventually the whole software stack can directly work on real hardware without any changes as soon as the first tape-out is ready.

title: ChiProgramBench: Can LLM Agents Rebuild Efficient Circuits from Pin-Level Experiments?
summary: Understanding a system that can be run but not inspected is a core engineering skill: one designs experiments, forms hypotheses about hidden state and timing, discards those that observations refute, and finally builds a replacement that works and is efficient. To evaluate this capability of LLM agents in the hardware domain, we present ChiProgramBench, 18 tasks derived from open-source processors, accelerators, codecs, transforms, interconnects, and control circuits. Agents can only drive and read the pins of a hidden, stateful simulated reference, then submit a gate-level netlist made of public library cells. Agents work in two settings: black-box discovery gives only anonymized functional pins and the interfaces of fixed memories, while function-guided reconstruction adds the circuit's purpose and each pin's role. Hidden test cases compare outputs with the reference cycle by cycle; power, delay, and area earn credit relative to the reference only when every case passes. Across 432 trials of 6 LLM agent configurations, successful agents recover algorithms and numerical conventions, yet only 12.0% of black-box and 14.8% of function-guided trials pass every case. Function-guided reconstruction raises the mean functional score, the cycle-weighted share of passed cases, from 24.6% to 30.9%. Of the 58 fully passing designs, only three improve on the reference's combined power, area, and delay, so behavioral recovery and efficient implementation remain distinct challenges.

title: X-BQSR: Holistic Acceleration of Base Quality Recalibration for Scalable Genomic Analysis
summary: With the continued decline in sequencing costs, genomics-based precision medicine is gaining increasing importance. The Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK) is the standard framework for converting raw genomic data into actionable variants, but one of its most expensive steps is base quality score recalibration (BQSR), which corrects systematic sequencing errors. Despite significant work on accelerating other parts of the variant calling pipeline, BQSR has not been systematically explored on GPUs. In this work, we analyze BQSR to identify computational and I/O bottlenecks and show that simply offloading key stages to an accelerator is insufficient to achieve overall gains. We then present X-BQSR, a holistic redesign of the entire BQSR pipeline, including I/O, compression, and kernel execution, to better leverage GPU parallelism. We implement X-BQSR using portable SYCL kernels for NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs, along with native CUDA and HIP backends for comparison, and we evaluate its performance against previous FPGA work. Our evaluation shows up to 141.7x acceleration compared to standard GATK and 8.7x acceleration compared to a proprietary GPU-accelerated solution.

title: Accurate Products, Inaccurate Inverse: Emulated FP64 BLAS in Blocked Triangular Inversion
summary: FP64 emulation on integer tensor units now ships in cuBLAS and GEMMul8, and each emulated matrix product can be checked against an accuracy grade. We ask if a routine built from such products inherits their accuracy, and show that blocked triangular inversion, the core of LAPACK's inverse of a symmetric positive definite matrix, does not. Under fixed-precision emulation every product passes the grade-B error bound of Demmel et al., yet the inverse errs at 7.1e-2, against 2.0e-15 natively. The matrices are well conditioned after diagonal scaling, but the scaling spans 64 binades. The cause is one product, T = X22 L21, whose summed index carries both the diagonal scaling and its inverse, which a grade-B bound does not absorb. Computing those products natively restores native accuracy; leaving any one of them emulated does not. The pattern holds on four GPUs, and on real covariance matrices the fixed-precision routes lose up to about four orders of accuracy. Equilibration, a solve-based association and cuBLAS's automatic dynamic precision avoid the loss, and an exact error recurrence audits a completed run. On an RTX 4090 the fastest accurate emulated inversion takes 0.40 of cuSOLVER's time. Where each product's scaling falls decides if per-product accuracy carries over to a composite routine, and that is what builders of emulated libraries need to check.

title: Closed-Form Formula for $d_{\mathrm{critical}}(a_0)$ in Large Fully Connected Power Grids
summary: Kadloor and Santhi (arXiv:1011.4098) modeled cascading failures in a large fully connected power grid by a coupled four-variable recursion for the minimum surviving load $a_n$, the mean failed load $μ_{n-1}$, the redistributed load $\mathcal{D}_n$, and the stagewise failure probability $p_n$. They noted that the recursion was not tractable and identified the critical disturbance $d_{\mathrm{critical}}$ by simulation. We show that the recursion telescopes exactly into a one-dimensional monotone map $a_{n+1} = g(a_n)$. This yields the threshold in closed form: $1 - a_0 = d_{\mathrm{critical}}\,(1 + \ln(1 + 1/d_{\mathrm{critical}}))$, or explicitly in terms of the lower branch $W_{-1}$ of the Lambert W function. We prove a sharp dichotomy. For $d_m \le d_{\mathrm{critical}}$ the cascade halts with limiting load $a_0 + d_{\mathrm{critical}}$ at criticality and surviving fraction $1/(1 + d_{\mathrm{critical}})$. For $d_m > d_{\mathrm{critical}}$ a complete outage occurs in finitely many steps.

title: High Throughput Meets Low Latency: CKKS Functional Bootstrapping on GPUs
summary: Functional (programmable) bootstrapping extends the bootstrapping operation of Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to evaluate an arbitrary function while refreshing a ciphertext. This capability was a unique feature of scalar CGGI/DM cryptosystems for many years until it was recently added to the toolset of vectorized FHE schemes, with CKKS being the most promising option both in terms of throughput (amortized time) and functionality. Previous work showed that CKKS functional bootstrapping outperforms CGGI/DM functional bootstrapping in terms of throughput by two to three orders of magnitude, but still loses in latency on CPU by two to three orders of magnitude. We present an optimized GPU implementation of CKKS functional bootstrapping that closes the latency gap. Our implementation supports evaluating functions over both small integers (as in CGGI/DM) and real numbers (unique to CKKS), which we call discrete-CKKS and continuous-CKKS functional bootstrapping, respectively.

title: SYCLDB: A Cross-Vendor Heterogeneous Analytical DBMS
summary: The rapid growth of AI and analytical workloads has increased the need for fast, interactive analytical data processing. This, in turn, has led to a surge of interest in designing accelerated analytical database engines that can exploit modern GPUs to scale computation. While GPUs provide the massive data-parallelism required by modern analytics, the software landscape remains dominated by closed-source, vendor-locked programming models, like CUDA, limiting portability across multi-vendor GPUs. In this work, we present SYCLDB, an end-to-end analytical database engine built upon the SYCL open standard, designed to enable efficient, hardware-agnostic execution across a wide range of accelerators using a single codebase. By implementing core relational operators as modular SYCL kernels, integrating them with a SQL frontend based on Apache Calcite and Apache Thrift, and supporting Apache Arrow for efficient columnar ingestion, SYCLDB reduces dependence on vendor-specific GPU programming stacks by enabling a single SYCL codebase to execute analytical query pipelines across Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA GPUs.

title: Which $\Diamond \mathcal{P}$ Algorithm is Suitable for You? An Empirical Benchmark on Real Network Traces
summary: Unreliable failure detectors (UFDs) are a fundamental abstraction for dependability and fault tolerance in distributed systems, supporting core distributed algorithms, such as consensus. Yet selecting a suitable detector remains difficult because existing implementations are evaluated under different environments, workloads, parameterizations, and quality-of-service (QoS) requirements. We address this problem by systematizing 14 $\Diamond \mathcal{P}$ and closely related $\Diamond \mathcal{P}$-style UFDs, implementing 13 of them, and providing a reusable benchmark for their empirical comparison. Our methodology evaluates detectors through common QoS metrics, such as detection time, mistake rate, and query accuracy, and combines same-input replay of network traces with live deployment for detectors whose active probing or cooperative behavior requires online execution. We then formalize failure-detector selection as a constrained algorithm-selection challenge, mapping operational requirements to suitable detector candidates. We instantiate this methodology under controlled variations of communication rate, host load, and crash regime. Applying the selection process shows that no detector is uniformly preferable across the evaluated settings. At relaxed detection-time budgets, 2W [Tomsic et al., IPDPS 2015] is the most frequently selected detector, appearing in 12 of 16 scenario-metric combinations for $T_D \le 500$ ms, whereas stricter budgets yield substantially more scenario- and metric-dependent selections. The benchmark and selection methodology provide a reusable basis for practical detector selection and for establishing stronger analytical baselines for future failure-detection approaches, including learning-based detectors.

title: Torcalia.jl: An MPI-based Runtime System for Asynchronous Task Parallelism in Julia
summary: Designed to address the two-language problem, the Julia programming language provides a powerful platform for developing high-performance scientific computing and machine learning applications. Such applications increasingly exhibit irregular, adaptive, or data-driven workloads for which traditional bulk-synchronous parallel (BSP) models often struggle to efficiently exploit the available parallelism. Asynchronous many-task (AMT) runtime systems offer a compelling alternative, decomposing computations into fine-grained tasks that are dynamically scheduled across the hierarchical architecture of modern HPC systems. This paper introduces Torcalia$.$jl, a Julia package designed to orchestrate the asynchronous execution of tasks across both shared and distributed memory environments. Built on top of MPI$.$jl and Julia's native multithreading, Torcalia employs a dependency-aware task scheduling scheme that combines the work-sharing and work-stealing paradigms to achieve adaptive load balancing. Tasks can be nested arbitrarily, enabling applications to exploit multiple levels of parallelism, while application-level distributed shared memory (DSM) extends task-based shared-memory programming to multi-node clusters. Beyond task-based programming, the proposed library supports skeletal programming, providing high-level abstractions that facilitate the implementation of parallel applications at scale. Evaluated on the ARIS supercomputer using four diverse workloads, Torcalia demonstrates strong scalability, reducing wall-clock time by up to 18.1% compared with Dagger, a state-of-the-art task-based engine in Julia. The source code of Torcalia$.$jl is publicly available at https://github.com/CEID-HPCLAB/Torcalia.jl.

title: Connected but Late: Sample Age of Commercial BLE Wearables under Wi-Fi Coexistence for Real-Time Clinical Applications
summary: Wearable sensors are increasingly being used in real-time clinical applications, such as rehabilitation robots and live therapy monitoring. As Healthcare 5.0 moves towards personalized therapies, their use will continue growing, potentially compromising communication reliability. Most wearables transmit over Bluetooth Low Energy, sharing 2.4 GHz with institutional Wi-Fi. Previous coexistence studies have focused on whether data arrive, rather than when. We measured sample age for a commercial electrocardiogram strap, from acquisition through the gateway to storage in our platform MEDWEAR, in an anechoic chamber and a hospital rehabilitation gym, and we compared it with illustrative clinical deadlines. Without load, the strap's own framing was the largest source of delay, making samples on average 280 ms and up to 550 ms old before transmission. Wi-Fi load had no measurable effect while adaptive frequency hopping could avoid the loaded channel. In a stress test, which forced the link onto the loaded channel, the link became the dominant source of delay, adding up to 11 s. The link stayed connected, but a median of 29% of samples and up to 98% (worst case) were older than 1 s on arrival at the gateway. The gym behaved mostly like the quiet chamber, but during one traffic burst, while hopping was restricted, up to 4.6% of samples were older than 1 s. These results show that a connected link can deliver late data. Therefore, sensors intended for real-time clinical applications should be profiled in situ and monitored based on sample age rather than connection status alone.

title: Bridging the Semantic Gap from Natural Language Specifications to RTL with Layered Formal Guidance
summary: While large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in generating register-transfer level (RTL) code from natural-language specifications, their reliability remains limited on designs with complex control logic and temporal behavior. This stems from a fundamental semantic gap: high-level natural language often leaves implementation-critical details underspecified, forcing LLMs to infer unstated assumptions. This paper presents Layered Formal Guidance, a novel framework that bridges this semantic gap by using formal properties as an intermediate semantic layer between natural-language specifications and RTL generation. Our framework applies formal guidance across three layers: property-driven specification augmentation before generation, property-consistency checking after generation, and counterexample-guided refinement after checking. Experiments on RTLLM benchmarks and various open-source IP designs demonstrate that our framework achieves higher functional correctness and lower sampled output-trace diversity. Furthermore, we show that Layered Formal Guidance can flexibly augment both general-purpose LLMs and domain-specific models to substantially improve their generation reliability.

title: Trustworthy Edge AI: Security, Privacy, and Resilience for Distributed Intelligence
summary: This chapter examines the principles and emerging research directions for building secure, privacy-preserving, and resilient Edge Artificial Intelligence (Edge AI) systems. As intelligence shifts from centralized clouds to distributed edge environments, challenges arise in ensuring data integrity, privacy, and reliable operation under adversarial and uncertain conditions. The chapter analyzes Edge AI architectures, emphasizing the expanded attack surface due to heterogeneous devices, resource constraints, and dynamic networks. It reviews core security mechanisms, including hardware-rooted trust, zero-trust models, secure communication, and attestation. Privacy-preserving approaches, such as federated learning, secure aggregation, and differential privacy, enable collaborative intelligence without centralized data sharing. Resilience strategies, including fault tolerance, adversarial robustness, and adaptive orchestration, are also explored. Case studies from smart cities, autonomous vehicles, healthcare, and industrial IoT illustrate practical trade-offs. The chapter advocates a holistic, cross-layer design integrating security, privacy, and resilience for trustworthy edge intelligence.

title: Stress2Twin: Profile-Driven Network Digital Twins for Guarded Edge Computing Resource Management
summary: Heterogeneous edge systems require resource managers to determine how many application replicas to deploy, where to place them, and how to distribute incoming requests while satisfying service-level performance constraints. Acquiring the performance knowledge required for these decisions through exhaustive multi-node characterization is measurement-intensive and becomes increasingly difficult as the number of workers and configurations grows. Stress2Twin is a profile-driven Network Digital Twin (NDT) framework that profiles edge nodes independently and composes their measured behavior into a system-level resource-management model. Machine-level oracles characterize latency, throughput, loss, queueing, and power as functions of assigned request rate and replica count. A guarded optimizer derives operating regions and tests neighboring request-rate states before retaining a replica count, reserving capacity before measured nonlinear degradation. Independent profiling of our three-worker Kubernetes testbed requires 271 measured states, corresponding to approximately 4.5 hours, compared with an estimated 123 hours for exhaustive characterization of the considered cluster configuration space. In a single-run ramp evaluation, the selected policy records no latency or loss-threshold violations within the derived 1,650 requests per second (RPS) supported range and reduces estimated power by 27.84% relative to RPS100 Round Robin (RR) placement. An additional single-run evaluation under a non-monotonic workload records no latency violation and 19.67% lower estimated energy than a stabilized RPS50 RR policy. These results show that independently acquired machine profiles can support capacity-aware resource consolidation within a measured operating range. Power savings use an idealized active-worker accounting model.

title: Teaching Time Without Losing General Retrieval: Adapting Multimodal Embeddings for Time-Sensitive Video Retrieval
summary: In text-to-video retrieval, MLLM-based embedding models do well when the text describes the scene (general retrieval), but poorly when it describes actions and their direction (time-sensitive retrieval). TARA, a pioneering work, fine-tunes such a model on text triplets with temporal hard negatives; it improves time-sensitive retrieval but lowers general retrieval (mean R@1 over six benchmarks in our rerun on Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B: 58.4->44.8), and its released model keeps general retrieval only when ensembled with Qwen3-VL-Embedding. Our goal is strong general and time-sensitive retrieval with one model and one vector per clip. Three findings lead to three simple components. Keep loss: general retrieval follows how far the output embeddings drift from the base model, not how far the weights move; we therefore keep them near the base model, which keeps most general retrieval even without general-domain data. Pair loss: the text embeddings of an action description and its reversed-direction version are well separated, but the video embeddings of a clip and its reversed copy are close; we therefore widen the gap between the video embeddings of each clip and its reversed copy, in the direction of the difference between their two text embeddings. Middle-layer LoRA: frames are combined in the middle layers, and temporal information peaks in or just after them; we therefore train LoRA only on these layers, which nearly matches training all weights on most time-sensitive benchmarks with 0.15% of the parameters and keeps general retrieval better. General R@1 stays at 58.4, while R@1 with each clip's reversed copy in the gallery rises from 55.5 to 63.2; the gains carry over to unseen benchmarks and InternVL2-8B-RA. The keep loss is also a remedy for the TARA recipe (general R@1: 44.8->57.8), and ensembling TARA with Ours gives the highest scores on RTime and unseen CiA among the compared models.

source.name: arXiv Embodied AI / Robotics / World Models

title: FocusAnchor: Zero-Shot Metric Depth by Anchoring a Depth Foundation Prior to Focus Cues
summary: Existing depth-from-focus methods can struggle with weak focus cues, new cameras, or fewer focal slices. We present FocusAnchor, a recurrent model that uses focus-volume lookups to refine metric depth and repeatedly aligns a relative depth prior from a frozen foundation model to the current depth estimate. The aligned prior guides subsequent refinement in a feedback loop, carrying metric scale recovered from textured regions into regions where focus cues are weak while preserving scene structure. To support transfer across cameras, we synthesize training stacks with randomized camera parameters and focus distances. However, stack synthesis blurs existing image noise differently across slices, creating artificial depth cues even on textureless surfaces. We add independent per-slice noise to suppress these cues. We also introduce variable-stack training to improve robustness with fewer focal slices and support more practical mobile capture. Compared with FOSSA ViT-B, FocusAnchor reduces AbsRel by 36% on NYU Depth V2 and by 9% on DDFF-12 after fine-tuning. In zero-shot evaluation, FocusAnchor and its variable-stack variant, FocusAnchor-flex, achieve the two lowest AbsRel values on all five benchmarks. On ZEDD test, FocusAnchor achieves 9% lower AbsRel than the best competing method, FOSSA ViT-B, while FocusAnchor-flex achieves lower AbsRel with 40% fewer focal slices on ZEDD validation.

source.name: arXiv Embodied AI / Robotics / World Models

title: Eliciting the Recall Capacity of Linear Attention
summary: Linear attention models exhibit a disproportionate deficit relative to softmax attention in associative recall (AR) in language modeling. We investigate this gap through natural language evaluations, synthetic recall tasks, and targeted training interventions. Using a synthetic setting, we quantify the role of state-size in how many items can be recalled from memory and find a similar empirical scaling across the tested linear-attention architectures. Testing this relationship reveals that even a single layer at scale can learn to retrieve thousands of associations across long distances. Yet, standard language model training does not reliably teach a linear model to copy from context, whereas a comparable softmax model learns to do so. Considering this, we strengthen recall supervision during training through in-context sentence repetition and context-sensitive loss reweighting. Both methods improve recall-intensive benchmark performance and narrow the long-distance AR gap to the softmax baseline without changing the architecture, token budget, or number of optimization steps, at a slight cost to general language modeling. These targeted changes to training can thus elicit substantial but underutilized retrieval capacity in linear-attention models. These findings suggest that, although linear-attention architectures have substantial capacity for recall, their inductive biases and the demands of language model training make it difficult to develop this capability without dedicated incentives.

source.name: arXiv Embodied AI / Robotics / World Models

title: VidForce: Predicting Force-Aware Articulation by Observing Humans
summary: People can anticipate how an object moves and the effort an interaction may require by watching others. How can embodied agents acquire this understanding from video? Force measurements provide direct sensory supervision, but require specialized equipment and remain limited in quantity. We introduce VidForce, which estimates an interaction trajectory together with a force profile from a third-person RGB video; 2D contact clicks and textual object-action prompts are optional. Our approach makes limited instrumented measurements useful for interpreting human interactions through learned physical prototypes as a prior. The prototypes share learned force levels and temporal profiles across interactions of comparable effort, with visual and semantic cues determining their contribution to each observation. Geometric and vision-language features adapt this prior to the observed interaction, while a joint conditional flow refines an initial tracked trajectory together with the force profile. Paired human and instrumented-gripper recordings provide measured force references for supervising human video, and a separately trained torque model demonstrates that the formulation extends to other sensory quantities. We evaluate trajectory recovery and force estimation through baseline comparisons and controlled ablations on held-out interactions from the Hoi! dataset. On this evaluation subset, VidForce achieves 6.6 cm ATE, peak-force MAE and RMSE of 4.81 N and 5.92 N, respectively, and force-profile RMSE of 5.52 N. On real-world videos, VidForce infers motion and force reliably and consistently despite the variability in human execution. We further deploy VidForce on a Spot robot, where trajectories and force profiles estimated from human demonstrations drive real-world articulated-object manipulation, and report success rates across repeated trials. Project page: https://rafaymhddn.github.io/vidforce

source.name: arXiv Embodied AI / Robotics / World Models

title: Benchmarking Evidence Sufficiency in Vision-Language Models for Autonomous Driving
summary: Reliable driving VLMs must do more than answer correctly or localize relevant scene actors: they must determine whether the available visual evidence is sufficient to support an answer. Existing evaluations largely treat grounding and answerability as separate measurements, making it difficult to distinguish well-supported predictions from those localized to relevant but insufficient evidence. We introduce DriveAnswer, a benchmark of 20,151 questions across seven reasoning families, that operationalizes this distinction using matched strong- and weak-evidence configurations. Each pair preserves the underlying scene fact and semantic answer while changing whether the observations support answering, making abstention the appropriate response under weak evidence. On the six-family evaluation, the strongest zero-shot baseline reaches 67.31% strong-evidence accuracy, yet only 21.55% of matched questions satisfy both answer-abstain behavior and complete grounding. With controlled adaptation, Gemma-4-12B reaches 63.29% on this joint capability, nearly tripling its zero-shot performance. Qwen3-VL-8B exhibits the same broad improvement in evidence-sensitive answering and grounding. These results show that semantic correctness, evidence sufficiency, and grounding are distinct capabilities that should be evaluated jointly.

source.name: arXiv Embodied AI / Robotics / World Models

title: From Safety-Driven Redundancy to Value-Driven Architecture: An ODD-Based Rationalization Framework for Level 4 Autonomous Vehicles
summary: Level 4 autonomous vehicles require fault-tolerant architectures that preserve critical driving functions under sensing, computing, communication, power, and actuation failures. As these systems progress toward industrial scalability, architectural complexity, validation burden, integration effort, and lifecycle cost become increasingly relevant. This study proposes an Operational Design Domain (ODD)-based, safety-constrained systems-engineering framework for architecture rationalization. ODD-specific capabilities, physical fault assumptions, post-fault operational policies, and spatial sensing requirements are propagated through an integrated safety-feasibility gate. Architecture transformations, including removal, relocation, functional reassignment, and consolidation, are evaluated only within the resulting safety-feasible design space, followed by lifecycle-cost sensitivity and robust multiobjective Pareto analysis. A generic, synthetically parameterized Level 4 architecture is used as a demonstrative computational case study.
